# Input Elicitation

**Version:** 0.1 · **Date:** 2 September 2026 · **First version:** 2 September 2026 · **Status:** For review
**How the craft is used in the conversation.** [discovery-craft](../../../specifications/definitions/know-how/method/discovery-craft.md) is what you know;
this is what you do with it while a person is in front of you. Assembled from the know-how survey,
its `interaction` register, and Horvitz's mixed-initiative principles.
**Parent contract:** [PILOT-BUSINESS-LOGIC.md](../../../specifications/PILOT-BUSINESS-LOGIC.md)
**Owner:** Česká spořitelna · **Written by:** Igor Tadić · **Read by:** `brief-creation` · `opportunity-framing`

> **What this is.** Getting a usable input out of somebody who has the answer and cannot easily phrase it.
> That is nearly everybody, for the reason [discovery-craft](../../../specifications/definitions/know-how/method/discovery-craft.md) §1 gives, and it is the
> hardest thing this workflow asks an agent to do.
>
> **What this is not.** Not how you speak, which is
> [agent-interaction](../../../specifications/definitions/know-how/writing/agent-interaction.md): batching, labelling a turn, reporting in outcomes,
> the receipt, and what an agent never does. That body owns the manner of the exchange. **This one owns
> its substance: what to ask, how to tell a good answer from a thin one, and what to do with each.**
>
> **And it is not a licence to answer for them.** Everything here makes it easier for a person to give you
> a real answer. Nothing here lets you write one down that they did not give.

---

## 1. Recognition is cheap and composition is expensive, so stop asking people to compose

**This is the operating consequence of the articulation barrier**, and it is the rule most of this body
turns out to be.

**Where the set of plausible answers is closed and small, offer it.** The run's language, whether a
participant is a direct competitor or a substitute, which of the bank's existing key results this moves.
A person picking from four is doing something they are good at. The same person writing the same answer
into an empty box is doing something most people are not.

**Offering is not inferring.** The value becomes theirs the moment they choose it, and the record already
says who decided.

**Where the set is open, propose nothing.** A root cause, a customer impact, an outcome statement, an
alternative to an opportunity, an ordering of anything. **A proposal into an open set is an anchor**, it
comes back as their answer with your wording on it, and the next stage then generates against it.

**An offer names more than one option, or names where the whole set can be seen.** *Here is X, confirm it
or choose another* is a proposal wearing an offer's clothes: **a person who has not seen the set cannot
choose another**, so the only move available to them is to agree. One first ask for the
bank's key result named one and invited another, and what came back was agreement with a set the person had
never been shown. Two or three, or a pointer to where they are all written down.

**A candidate you offer must be consistent with what they have already told you.** The same run proposed a
key result sitting under the business-clients objective one turn after the segment had been set to retail.
**Check a candidate against the answers already on the record before it is offered**, not after it comes back
as theirs — an offer that contradicts an earlier answer asks a person to catch your mistake, and they
usually will not.

**The line, stated once so it can be applied without rereading this.** Closed and enumerable: offer, more
than one, consistent with what they have said. Open and generative: describe the shape and wait.

---

## 2. Never open into empty space

**Open an elicitation with three things before the first question.** What this stage decides. What it does
not decide, and who does that instead. The list of what you need, with a count.

**An open question into nothing taxes the one skill a product manager was not hired for**, and it is the
most expensive first move available. *Tell me about the problem* is that move.

**Then name each field in their language, say what it is for, and say what it changes downstream.**

> *What is the outcome this initiative is meant to produce? Not what we would build, but what changes for
> the customer. The whole run hangs off it: the problems we dig into and the market we look at are chosen
> against this sentence.*

That is one exchange. *What is the outcome?* is the same field and a worse answer.

**They should never have to ask you what you mean.** Where they do, you left it out.

---

## 3. Say what a good answer looks like, one line per question

**Most unanswered questions are unanswered because nobody knew what was wanted.**

**Build every example from a different case.** An example drawn from their own situation is an anchor and
comes back as their answer. *Another team put a named decision and a date here, something like whether
this enters the Q1 portfolio, decided in November* anchors nothing and shows the shape.

**Run the disambiguation test before sending.** A colleague reading the question alone, with none of this
conversation, should be able to say what answer is wanted. If they could not, it is not a question yet.

### 3.1 What a good answer looks like, by input

**This table is knowledge, not a script.** It is here so you can describe the shape in one line and
recognise the weak version when it arrives.

| Input | A good one | The weak version, and what to ask next |
|---|---|---|
| **The outcome** | A change in customer behaviour, stated as a change | A thing to build. Ask what would be different for the customer once it exists |
| **The decision this feeds** | A named decision with a date | *We want to explore the area.* Ask who takes the decision this informs, and when |
| **The customer** | A segment doing something specific in a specific situation | A demographic. Ask what they are trying to get done and where it goes wrong |
| **What is at stake for them** | What they stand to gain or lose, which is what makes friction tolerable | Silence. Ask what happens to them if they do not finish. Severity cannot be sized without it |
| **The success signal** | A number with an owner, or a named unknown with an owner | A direction. Ask which existing key result this moves, and offer the list |
| **Scope** | What is out, said plainly | Only what is in. Ask what is deliberately not in this |
| **The material** | What customers said or did, with when and where each came from | A strategy deck. Take it as background, say it is background, and say it is not a problem set |

**For the outcome specifically, the canon holds eight named ways of stating one badly**
([method-canon](../../../specifications/definitions/know-how/method/method-canon.md) §9.2), each with its remedy. Read them there and use them as
the diagnosis rather than repeating the question.

---

## 4. Read what they actually gave you before asking for more

**Three things arrive looking like the answer and are not**, and each has a different opening back.

**A solution where a problem was asked for.** *Customers need a progress indicator.* Do not reject it and
do not accept it. **Ask what it would fix**, and the problem comes out in their words.

**A feeling where a behaviour was asked for.** *They find it confusing.* Ask what they saw somebody do
that made them say it.

**An output where an outcome was asked for.** *Launch the mobile flow.* Ask what would be different for a
customer once it is launched.

**In all three the person gave you something real.** They answered the question one layer down from where
you needed it, which is what a person does when the question was one layer up from where they think. **The
move is a follow-up, never a correction**, and never a rewrite of their words into better ones.

---

## 5. When they cannot answer, that is an answer

**Record it as unknown with the reason and who would normally hold it, or name the later stage that
produces it. Then move on.** Do not ask twice, and do not let it end the stage.

**Account for every item you asked about.** A question raised and left is different from a question nobody
raised, and only one of them tells a later reader anything. **The fact that you asked belongs in the note
beside the reason.**

**A batch you do not close is a drip that loses the drops.** A stage offered five
fields in one message, the person answered one, and the other four are absent from the brief, absent from
the unknowns and absent from the bounds. The person had answers. Nothing anywhere records that they were
asked.

---

## 6. Before asking again, say what would change

**State what the run already holds against the question, and what a new answer would alter. If nothing
would alter, do not ask.**

**Their willingness to answer is the scarce input in this workflow**, more than their time and much more
than yours. A round that changes nothing spends it, and the next round is answered worse.

**This is Horvitz's rule from 1999 and it has not been improved on:** use dialogue to resolve the
uncertainties that matter, act where the value of acting clears the cost of guessing wrong, and design so
that a wrong guess is cheap to undo. **A question is a cost. Ask when it buys more than it costs.**

---

## 7. When they ask you to help them figure it out, help

**A person saying help me work this out is asking you to think with them, and you are permitted to.** Ask
what would make the answer obvious. Offer two or three shapes the answer could take. Say what other
initiatives usually put there. **Then let them say it in their own words and record theirs.**

**Say which one you would pick, when they ask you.** *The activated-products result is the closest,
because that is the same event as a card being activated* is a view, and a view is the thing they asked
for. **Then stop.** They choose, the record carries their choice, and you do not add that it is their call
rather than yours. They know, and a disclaimer on a view is a way of not having given one.

**Inventing a fact and holding an opinion are different acts.** The no-inference rule exists to stop the
first: a segment, a metric, a constraint nobody stated. It was never meant to stop you saying which of two
real options fits better, and a reading that forbids both leaves the person doing the work alone.

### 7a. Strategic alignment is the one step where this is the default rather than the response

**Everything above waits to be asked. This step does not.** When the run reaches how the initiative aligns
to what the bank is already trying to do, lead with the elaboration rather than holding it back:

- **The plausible key results, with the reasoning for and against each**, not a list of names.
- **Two or three shapes a north star could take** for an initiative like this one.
- **A failing example before a passing one.** *An improvement a person reviewing the data would call
  material* has no threshold, no owner and no moment, so nobody can tell whether it was met. Show that
  first, then what it looks like when it carries one.

**The reason: this is a selling point of the stage, and without the offer it
sits behind a question nobody knows to ask.** A person meeting this workflow for the first time does not
know that asking would produce any of the above, so the help arrives only for someone who already knew it
was there.

**§7 governs every other step unchanged.** This is one step, named, and the change is when the elaboration
arrives rather than what it contains.

---

## 8. Say so once when something looks wrong

**One sentence they can check, then take their answer.** *That north star is the same sentence as your
outcome, which means this run has no broader direction above it. Is that right?*

**Repeating it after they have answered is not useful.** Where their answer stands and your reading
differs, the record keeps theirs and notes that yours was offered.

---

## 9. What you never do here

**Fill a field nobody supplied.** Everything in this body exists to make a real answer easier to give.
None of it makes an absent one acceptable to write.

**Rewrite their words into better ones.** Their phrasing of the outcome, the audience and the scope is
authoritative. You may sharpen a supplied input only by saying what you derived it from and staying
strictly inside it. **An unmarked substitution is refused**, and a sharpening that adds a fact is marked
unknown instead.

**Let material overrule the person.** Where a supplied document asserts a different audience or scope,
that is one item about a source, and the brief is unchanged.

**Ask for a value the machinery owns.** A path, a field name, a format. Those are not
theirs to give.

---

## 10. Coverage bar

Its readers are `brief-creation` and `opportunity-framing`. **A predicate such as every
skill that asks a person for anything is wider than the two bindings** — the Methodology Coach asks
clarifying questions and does not declare this body. Recorded rather than resolved here.

| Question | Where | Could a check decide it |
|---|---|---|
| When to offer candidates and when to propose nothing | §1 | No |
| How an elicitation opens | §2 | No |
| What a good answer looks like per input | §3 | No |
| What to do with a solution, a feeling or an output where something else was asked | §4 | No |
| What happens when they cannot answer | §5 | **Partly.** The unknown mark and its reason are fields |
| When to ask a second time | §6 | No |
| What help is permitted when they ask for it | §7 | No |
| What is never done | §9 | **Partly.** A filled field with no source is what the run record already exposes |

**Assessment: nothing in this body is observable, and that is a property of the subject rather than a gap
in the writing.** No instrument in this build reads a conversation. The only record a session leaves is
the editor's own chat journal, and the trace export this repository enrols has never produced a file.

**So the honest bar is the one [agent-interaction](../../../specifications/definitions/know-how/writing/agent-interaction.md) §12 states.** A skill
declaring this body has read it. Nothing checks that it obeyed, and the measurement behind that sentence
is that a skill with the interaction body loaded broke three of its sections in a single stage.

---

## 11. Open

| # | Question | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **E-a** | §3.1 names what is at stake for the customer and no brief field carries it | Either `brief-fields` gains one, or the question is asked well and the answer lands where nothing reads it |
| **E-b** | §1's closed-set rule and the alternatives section, which stays empty on purpose | They agree today because an alternative is an open set. Worth restating if a stage ever offers a closed list of them |
| **E-c** | §5 requires every asked item to be closed, and the reasons are a fixed set of four | *Offered, not answered* is not one of the four. It goes in the note beside the reason, and a check cannot tell the two apart |
